newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian city of traditional revolt escapes turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Albanian city of traditional revolt escapes turmoil.

text.p: The north Albanain city of Shkoder, for centuries a hotbed of revolt against authority, has been spared the violence now surging through the south.

Officials say the neat city of 80,000, home to Roman Catholics, Moslems and Orthodox, has avoided being pitched into the bloodletting by cool heads and less exposure to the excesses of six years of post-communist rule.

Mayor Bahri Borici, who represents a coalition grouping right-wingers and monarchists, said on Tuesday he believed keeping his administration free of officials of President Sali Berisha's ruling Democratic Party had helped keep the peace.
"The people in power here are from parts of society which suffered greatly under the former Communist regime," he told Reuters.

"When this revolt started, all parties and religious communities united to try to keep the damage to a minimum. The message from City Hall was 'Keep violence away from here!'. Damaging property means only damaging ourselves."

On the bustling streets of the city, which hugs Lake Shkoder, a nature reserve stretching into Montenegro, token police roadblocks are the only evidence that a national state of emergency has been in force for more than a week.
But tension lies fairly close to the surface.
"You think about it all the time. There are plenty of rumours," said Eglantina, an office worker in her forties. "God, let them not bring that disorder and tragedy here!"

Most scoff at suggestions that the conflict, sparked by the collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes, is linked to traditional rivalry between ethnic groups speaking different dialects -- Gegs in the poorer north and Tosks in the south.

"It was different here with pyramids. People had only small amounts to invest compared to southern towns like Vlore," said Lefter Kashta, a biology professor at Shkoder University who moved 25 years ago from Vlore, a focal point of the unrest.
"And people were less exposed to some of the bad influences of the West. There was none of the drug trade or trafficking in emigrants across to Italy like down there."

The region may have had less access to lucrative business across the Adriatic. But locals took full advantage of the opportunities accorded by the embargo against Serbia during the Bosnia war to transport oil illegally northward.

The relative calm in the city, 120 km (75 miles) north of the capital Tirana on potholed roads, belies a tradition of resistance to authority dating from an unsuccesful six-year campaign to keep out Turkish invaders in the late 15th century.
Shkoder residents fought against Serbian forces in 1912 and revolted against Albania's King Zog 14 years later.
It was the only city to mount a futile anti-communist revolt in the aftermath of World War Two and was in the forefront of 1990-91 protests that toppled communist rule.

Residents say the frenzied attacks on troops and police in the south are unthinkable in a town where different ethnic and religious groups live side by side. Armed rebels demand Berisha's resignation and accuse him of failing to warn unwary investors of the dangers of the investment schemes.

"People here have always supported each other. Tolerance has been a watchword," said Don Jozef Buka, 71, a deacon at Shkoder's 19th century painted stone cathedral who served 12 years in prison under Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha.
"People in the south thought they could make quick money with dirty things like drugs. People here were more apt to work together, Moslems and Christians, even at fighting the Turks."

The cathedral was closed by Hoxha in 1967, like all Albania's churches, and made into a basketball arena. Shkoder's Catholics, 40 percent of the population, reclaimed it in 1990 and had it ready for Pope John Paul's visit three years later.
Most residents took the bloodshed in the south to heart.
"Forget the north-south divide. My husband is a southerner, my children are their brothers and sisters," said Hiqmete, 45, a worker at a fishmonger's. "Their problems are our problems."
